name: New York Pink
lede: New York Pink is a dusty, brownish pink from Wikipedia's color lists, named for the city rather than any pigment or dye.

sections.title: A city, not a hue
sections.body:
New York Pink carries #D7837F, the exact value Wikipedia's color lists give for it, filed under "shades of pink" [1]. Our library finds no earlier record and no explanation of why New York earned a pink of its own; the name is a place word applied to a hue, not a dye or trade good [1][2].

The nearest named colors on file are [[grecian-rose]], [[pink-coral]], [[old-rose]] and [[peach-rose]], at 3.2, 3.2, 4.3 and 4.3 ΔE [2]. In ISCC-NBS terms it reads as a dark yellowish pink, and in Munsell notation 4.9R 6.3/7.7 [2]. 2, 3.2, 4.3 and 4.3 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this pink in 42 of 23,781 paintings, 0.18 percent, rarer than 65 percent of our named colors, as photographed [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 5 of 1,674 paintings, but on only five paintings, three times the same museums' baseline rate [3]. Where the within-painting lens finds it (14 paintings), it plays an accent in 64 percent of them rather than a light or shadow [3]. The earliest dated example is a 1398 panel by Paolo di Giovanni Fei and the latest is from 1916; our early centuries are thin, so that date is a floor, not a first [3]. These are color matches in photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [3].

questions.q: What is New York Pink named after?
True or false: our sources explain why this pink is tied to New York.

openers: New York Pink is named for a city, not for anything pink was ever made from.

issues: Editor spot-audit 2026-10-09: added the n=5 behind the 1900s peak, the n=14 base for the accent share, the floor-not-first caveat on 1398, and fixed 'brownish-pink a shade duller still' (it is 4.3 away, not duller than Grecian Rose).
